utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good morning. The Chamber is seized of the Prosecution's motion for the testimony of a certain witness to be heard via videolink. I was told that the Defence is in a position to respond to this motion orally. Are you, Mr. Tolimir, prepared to respond this morning in the courtroom? Mr. Tolimir doesn't have a proper translation. Mr. Gajic, did you receive interpretation? The problem is solved, I was told.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I hope so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I have to repeat. Is the Defence in a position to respond to this Prosecution's motion? Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. We will give our oral response. If I'm not mistaken, it concerns a Prosecution motion of the 18th of March of this year concerning a witness; I don't know if it's a protected witness so I don't want to mention his name. In any case, the Defence position is that we will leave it entirely in your hands. I was only asked by Mr. Tolimir to tell you that the only thing we don't want to happen is that this videolink testimony becomes standard practice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I think there is no -- there's no need for being worried because we have up to now heard nearly 100 witnesses and this is the first time that the Prosecution filed such a motion. The Chamber will consider the application.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The Prosecution's motion of the 18th of March in relation to Witness Ramiz Husic, he is not a protected witness, is granted. The necessary arrangements should be made. The witness should be brought in, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good morning, sir. Please sit down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Welcome back to the courtroom. Thank you for your patience. I have to remind you that the affirmation to tell the truth still applies. Mr. Tolimir is continuing his cross-examination. Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. May peace reign in this house. I'd like to greet everyone including Mr. Smith, and may today's proceedings be concluded in keeping with God's will and not my own.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Smith, yesterday we discussed all of the topics concerning Zepa. You mentioned that I was involved with some prisoners on a number of occasions, thus hindering an exchange all-for-all. Do you recall having stated that and that you wished to discuss it further?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall stating it that you were hindering an exchange in the way that you've expressed it there, and I certainly didn't say I wanted to discuss it any further.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Then I apologise. Yesterday I asked you if you recalled those prisoners you mentioned returned immediately prior to crossing over to Muslim-held territory and that that piece of information arrived from the command of the forces in charge of the operation. The information was to the extent that the Muslims refused to surrender. It was on the 28th. Were you familiar with that?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: You -- I'm not familiar with the particular issue that you're discussing. I don't know this case, the particular case that you're talking about. I would need reminding and then I might find I knew. But I don't see how this is connected with the previous question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I will try to make the link.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please see D173 which is Edward Joseph's statement. Page 4, paragraph 19. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: We can see the statement and we'll look at para 19 in both versions. I will read it out. I quote Mr. Joseph: "The previously-mentioned group of slightly wounded men boarded probably the last bus. I recall them being a group of 12. As they were of military age, they were problematic in terms of evacuation. Viktor and I went to General Tolimir of the VRS who was in this area of the centre of town. I asked him if he would allow these 12 to go through the Serb-controlled territory without being disturbed and he clearly replied yes." This is probably the group in question. You received information from your associates that I approved for them to leave and that the group was later returned. I wanted to ask you this: Did you know that this group on the last day, the 28th, was returned from the separation line between Muslims and Serbs in Kladanj where they were supposed to cross over into ABiH territory because it was at that point in time that we learned that not all Muslims wished to lay down their weapons, and it was then ordered that any further implementation of the agreement be halted?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know that what you have just stated had occurred, nor do I have any evidence that it did occur. All I reported in my statement, as I recall it, is that I was told that you had removed a number of people from a bus, that is to say, a number of wounded soldiers from a bus.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you know that General Mladic ordered for all those who came to Zepa handing over their weapons be exchanged and the same thing went for all those who were implementing the agreement in full and abiding by his instructions?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not know it as you have stated it there. I knew that we were evacuating these people. And my understanding was that once they were on the bus, they were clear to go.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell us this, please, your personnel in Zepa monitoring and assisting with the evacuation, did they report to you that anyone was held in Zepa by the VRS and that someone was prevented from leaving?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Amongst others I was told that you were holding Palic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. We will see that. There were witnesses here testifying to that effect.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us see the list which is P434 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: While we're waiting for it, can you tell us whether you knew that Palic was held by the VRS following the entire evacuation and that he was taken to Boksanica? He was then handed over, but not to me; he was handed over to the Rogatica Brigade.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: My memory of what I knew at the time was that he was -- I was not allowed to see him or talk to him and that my understanding is that he had probably been shot.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. When you were there he was probably still with the convoy because he escorted each and every one. We will see now that he was not finally killed and we'll see that in Mr. Bezruchenko's report once we are done with the document I initially asked for. Have a look at this document, please, and the list of POWs. It's an OTP document. All those who were held back following the Muslim refusal to honour the agreement and that they were all registered by the ICRC on the 28th. They were all put in a jail. I'm reading the first paragraph: "Since the 28th of July, 1995, the following Muslims have a status of prisoners of war placed in the military holding centre in Rogatica:" The following persons are on the list. We see them here.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please go to the next page for the witness to see. We can even go to page 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Forty-five persons so far. Let's go to the next page, please. There is a reference to their health in item B. And then we can see that they were all accommodated there, including Avdo Palic, in the penultimate paragraph. The pseudonym used for him is "Atlantis," as the OTP stated when presenting this document. It's stated here that he was placed in a different location.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we go to the last page of the document now.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: This was drafted by Captain Zoran Carkic. He also referred to Avdo Palic and he stated that they were all registered on the 28th. In this report we can also see, if we look at the penultimate paragraph, that some people had their personal items taken away and that I personally ordered an investigation in order to establish who took away their possessions so that the person in question could be appropriately sanctioned. It reads as follows: "The above-mentioned Muslims complained to General Tolimir and myself, saying that it was done by men under the command of a short man with black hair wearing a black beret and limping. It is obvious that it is Lieutenant Matic, who at the moment of separation of the Muslims came to the spot and carried out searches in the school and in the yard of the school. General Tolimir demanded that this case be investigated and money found." Given that the person in question was from the Drina Corps who was Carkic's superior, I personally requested of him to specifically mention my request in the report. Did you know that on the 28th all of them were placed in detention, registered by the ICRC, and put on a list?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't. I knew that the ICRC, who had no responsibility to report to me, but they had told me that they had seen some people at about this time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: We will have a look at what Mr. Bezruchenko had to say about it, who was there.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is D55.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: He stated that everyone was informed --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's look at paragraph 117 of the document before us. "The Fall of Zepa" drafted by Mr. Bezruchenko as an investigator of the OTP. It is page 33, paragraph 117.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: On the 28th of July, the commander of the 285th Brigade Avdo Palic was in VRS custody as General Tolimir reported that the 285th Brigade commander Avdo Palic provided information about the minefields in Zepa." In the footnote he refers to a particular document; it is footnote 174. Did Mr. Bezruchenko tell you that Avdo Palic was detained on the 28th? Could you have heard that from him?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I -- where does that -- where is the bit about --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We should go back one page in the English.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: May we have paragraph 117 again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Ah, I've got you. No, he didn't tell me, and I don't know that he knew that on the 28th of July. He's compiling a report of reports. I don't know when he found out the information in paragraph 117. It certainly doesn't say that he knew it on the 28th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you know that Mr. Edward Joseph testified that he followed the vehicle in which Mr. Avdo Palic was taken to Boksanica from the centre of Zepa? He stated that he was with Bezruchenko. They were with Avdo Palic up until the moment he was handed over to the Rogatica Brigade.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know that, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, good morning. I'd like a transcript cite for that proposition. If I understood it correctly, the General's position, what he's putting to this witness, is that Ed Joseph and Viktor Bezruchenko were with Avdo Palic until he was turned over to the Rogatica Brigade. I'd like a transcript cite for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, are you able to provide us with a reference?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I can't provide you with that. I recall what Mr. Joseph said while testifying; he said that Avdo Palic was arrested in the UNPROFOR base and was then taken to Boksanica hill. He also stated that he and Bezruchenko followed the vehicle. I just wanted to ask him about that particular detail, whether they told General Smith of their knowledge of Palic's arrest. As for his exact words, I can't quote them now. I just wanted to know whether they conveyed that information to him since they were on the spot. The witness is now saying they did not. Perhaps someone else could locate that particular transcript page. I could go back through my notes, given sufficient time though.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, you just said, "The witness is now saying they did not." This was not the answer of the witness. The witness said he doesn't know and didn't know, if I recall correctly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I knew that Palic had been taken by the Bosnian Serbs. That ... someone told me that. It could have been Joseph or Viktor. But what I don't know is the -- is the point that, you know, I do not know it in the form that the question was posed to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Indeed. That was my understanding of your answer. Mr. Tolimir, it is always helpful for the parties and the Chamber to give a reference from which part of the transcript or document you are quoting or referring. Therefore, please bear that in mind. Continue, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I will gladly do so at the earliest possible opportunity. I can't come up with it right now. I'm sorry. Could we now go back to one of the documents we saw a moment ago. In Mr. Bezruchenko's report, we referred to paragraph 123 yesterday, I believe. Could we please have it on the screen to jog the witness's memory. I won't quote from it. I simply have a question about it and about the detainees held by the Rogatica Brigade. We can see paragraph 123 now.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: We could see that according to the Muslim sources of the 30th of July everyone had pulled out from Zepa. You can recall the document we saw stating that they went to Serbia, et cetera. My question is this: If they had all left from the protected area in Zepa as stated by Bezruchenko based on ABiH documents and if they were all registered in the detention unit as referred to in P1434, which we just saw because we could see their first and last names, there were 35 -- sorry, 45 registered prisoners, then is there a possibility that the representatives of UNPROFOR and civilian authorities were not in Rogatica on the 28th and that the ICRC was? The ICRC registered them? Did you know that en route to Rogatica one needs to pass by that detention facility?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me answer the last question first. I knew that there was the -- a possible site, detention site, in Rogatica and that you would pass it. I don't -- I can't speak for the ICRC and what dates they were there. They are an independent body. And I don't know if the civil affairs people from UNPROFOR were there on the 28th or not. What I can say is that I was trying to make sure that every person in Zepa was accounted for and so I would like to think that my people and the ICRC were trying to locate these people and register them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: For the clarity of the record, Mr. Tolimir, you just mentioned P1434. In fact, we saw the document P434. Probably you misspoke. Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I must have misspoken. I often do that, permutations of numbers. The number is as you had put it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Smith. Were you informed that after the 30th, as paragraph 23 [as interpreted] says and as the army wrote, there were no soldiers or civilians left in Zepa after the 30th? Did you have information to that effect from any source whatsoever? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember with the precision as to the dates. We'd have to look at the documents coming from my headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. At any rate, can you answer the question? On the 30th were there any Muslims in Zepa? The 30th of August, were there any soldiers or were there any civilians there? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you mean August or July?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: August, August. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think there were any civilians in Zepa on the 30th of August, that is to say, Bosnian civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I promised you the day before yesterday that I would show you a document which shows that on the 30th of August you bombed the hill of Zlovrh in Zepa and you could not remember that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So I would now like to ask for 1D689 to be displayed in e-court. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, perhaps it is a translation issue. I don't think that it is appropriate to say "you bombed" the mount Zlovrh.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: UNPROFOR allowed the bombing using NATO air force. Now we're going to show what the document says. I accept your suggestion and your words of caution, thank you. As this document has not been translated, I would read out part of the first paragraph. This is what it says; this is a report of the command of the 1st Podrinje Light Brigade, that's the Rogatica Brigade, of the 30th of August, 1995. It was sent to the command of the Drina Corps and it is entitled, "Regular Combat Report." And it says: "This morning around 2.30 NATO air force bombed a facility which -- in which the centre for communications was stationed previously at Zlovrh. The Ustashas had torched the facility and over the past 10 days it was used for -- for our unit which was searching and checking the territory with a view to mopping up remaining enemy forces in the former enclave of Zepa. At the moment of the air-strikes in the building, there were a total of 14 soldiers. In the immediate vicinity, three air-bombs fell. One such bomb hit the building itself and as a result 10 soldiers in the building were killed, whereas four soldiers survived, however they were seriously injured." And then the soldiers who were killed are listed. Please, can you respond. Why was Zlovrh bombed at that point in time? Why were these soldiers killed when in Srebrenica -- sorry, I misspoke, Zepa, when in Zepa on the 30th of August there weren't any Muslim forces there, the evacuation was over? This is one month later. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: The -- as I said two days ago, I think it was, I don't recall the targets that were attacked on the 30th of August or, for that matter, the complete argumentation as to why they were chosen. This particular series of attacks had no direct relation to the enclave of Zepa itself. It was to do with the mortaring of Sarajevo and the consequence -- the actions that took place thereafter were a consequence of the decisions made at the London conference which were communicated to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. This is my question: Is Zepa in the immediate vicinity of Sarajevo? How far away is it, do you know? And can Sarajevo be mortared from Zepa? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: The answer to your questions is, no, it's not in the vicinity of Sarajevo; I do not know how far away it is; and with the weapons available to the Bosnian Serb forces, you couldn't mortar Sarajevo from Zepa. However, you are not hearing or taking account of my answer to the previous question. You have to recall what you were told about the decisions of the London conference to properly answer or to frame the questions that you're asking.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I had asked you whether the decisions of NATO and of the London conference were verified by the Security Council and you said that you did not remember. Do you remember today perhaps, and do you have a different answer today compared to yesterday? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I do not recall if they were verified by the Security Council. And the NATO decisions weren't made at the London conference.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Were procedures changed regarding air support, air-strikes, et cetera, at the London conference? Were procedures for making decisions on air-strikes, protection, et cetera, were they changed? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I've told you, the decision was made to put the authority to initiate air-strikes into the hands of the military commanders and in NATO and the UN, and the force commander was, as it were, given back the key.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. If you were given a key, did that mean that you could hit Republika Srpska at random or did you have to abide by a certain procedure in terms of target selection? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Targets were chosen -- were not chosen at random.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. This target in Zlovrh where there were no Muslim forces whatsoever and where there was no conflict at all, was it chosen randomly? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've just said they were not chosen at random. And we were not attacking the Muslim forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I understand that, that you were not attacking Muslim forces, because they were co-operative. This was a co-operative democracy that punished only those who were not co-operative. Could you please tell us why you did not target Muslim forces? And there were more reasons for that; there were more attacks in Zepa itself against UNPROFOR and in terms of the disarming of UNPROFOR, everything we discussed yesterday. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were not attacking Muslim forces because they had not violated the safe area of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Yesterday I read out a document to you. When they disarmed an entire Ukrainian company in Gorazde, was that not reason enough to bomb them?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: And I explained that it was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Do the procedures say that you can use fire-power only against targets from which there was firing in order to protect the forces that are carrying out the air-strikes and that are asking for air support by way of their own self-defence? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they didn't say that. And let me say it again: After the London conference, the decisions made -- and let me start again. At the London conference, the decisions that were made was that should a safe area and in particular attack on the civil population in a safe area occur, then air power was to be used and to be initiate -- and the use of it to be -- it was to be initiated by the military commanders. And air power would be used to enforce, if I recall the correct -- the words correctly, that until the safe area was and the exclusion zones around it were fully re-established.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have document 1D686 now. Let us see what it says regarding legal grounds for NATO operations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, are you tendering the document we -- you have just used and which was on the screen, 1D689?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I thought of tendering it. Thank you. I would kindly ask that it be admitted. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be marked for identification pending translation.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter document 1D689 shall be assigned Exhibit D187 marked for identification pending translation. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Can we now have 1D686 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: This is a document of the BH command for Sarajevo. It was written on the 15th of August, 1994. It had to do with heavy weaponry in various locations where it was kept so that it wouldn't be used. Thank you. We see it now on our screens. Let us now please look at the second paragraph of this document. I'm going to read it out: "At the present moment there is no legal basis (NAC resolution) for any NATO action against weapons outside the TEZ firing into the TEZ unless they are firing at targets inside Sarajevo city. NATO air-strikes -- air attacks can only be used against confirmed heavy weapons within the TEZ that are not withdrawn on order or endangering the security of UNPROFOR personnel." Thank you. On the basis of this, this is my question: Was any member of UNPROFOR or any safe area under threat from the hill of Zlovrh? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can I see the rest of this document, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. It's a very lengthy document; it has ten pages. It is ten pages long. I will let you take a look at it during the break and then we can discuss it once we are back from the break.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Could you please just say whether at the moment of attack was any UNPROFOR unit or any member of UNPROFOR, any safe area, endangered from Zlovrh? You can say that without reading the document, can you not?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- the -- they were not directly endangered by forces in that position of Zlovrh. But I keep coming back to the point that that isn't the basis on which the actions at the end of August were undertaken. It was based on the decision made at the London conference, which allowed for a much wider interpretation of the exclusion zone policy. Which was communicated to you and your headquarters either at the end of -- by the end of July or early August.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Smith. I said that we would continue discussing the legal basis for the application of force once you read the document. I am just asking about what happened at Zlovrh when ten soldiers were killed and four wounded. Was that the case or was it something else? Was it retaliation?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not clear what the question ... You were discussing a particular case and you were asking me about targeting decisions, and I thought I'd answered that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. What was not interpreted to you is whether this was retaliation; that's the word I used. Retaliation. Is that why Zlovrh was targeted?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I've said to you, I cannot recall the argumentation behind the choice of the targets in -- at the end of August.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. We see that today a decision was made to stop all air-strikes in Libya and on the other hand each and every mortar in Libya is being hit; is this part of that co-operative policy or is it about something else? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Again, like yesterday, I would remind you that we are only dealing in this case with events happening in the former Yugoslavia. If you need a discussion of principles, you should do that, but not in relation to any event happening around the world.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I just asked -- I mean, the point was co-operative democracy that is being introduced by way of tomahawks. Egypt, Lebanon, Yugoslavia, Bosnia; those are the examples I wanted to give. It is very important for this case why Republika Srpska was bombed. Was it bombed because it was not co-operative vis-à-vis NATO members that had air power or was it bombed for some other reason. Well, thank you, I understand you. I'm not going to ask if it has nothing to do with this case, but it does have something to do with this case. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Sir, can you answer the question? This was the essence of your argument: Was it bombed because it was not co-operative vis-à-vis NATO members that had air power or was it bombed for some other reason? That was the essence of the question. Perhaps you are able to answer this question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can say that the actions of the UN and NATO at the end of August were a direct result and reaction to the mortaring of the marketplace in Sarajevo which killed a large number of civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. You just mentioned the Sarajevo marketplace. Do you perhaps recall the letter that General Mladic sent to you in which he told you that a commission was being established that would investigate how come the explosion took place in the marketplace?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can recall exchanges with General Mladic at that time which included the idea of establishing a Joint Commission.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you recall your own communique and Mladic's communique and all the communiques then, namely that at the time no one knew who had fired the shell? And your assumption was -- or, actually Mladic said in his letters to you that no one fired this shell, that it was the Muslims themselves who committed this massacre in order to open the door for NATO to strike?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't make any assumptions. I carried out my own investigation, and I decided beyond reasonable doubt that the Bosnian Serbs had fired the mortar rounds that had killed these people.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Smith. Please, were you a ballistics expert? Could you conduct an investigation yourself without ballistics experts and without the warring parties that could contribute to an all-embracing high-quality investigation? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not a ballistic expert. I -- however, I was the competent authority and the person that was required to decide, and I had a staff to support me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Smith. Do you cover every decision on the basis of that competent authority, or should there be arguments and proof that would make it possible for you to resort to force? Because that is not a minor matter. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are we now talking generally or about that specific case?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. We were talking about this specific case where -- and a comprehensive investigation should have been carried out so that there would not be all these manipulations so many years later to this day because the investigation had not been completed. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am content with the decisions that I made at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Smith. Did you know beforehand what would be bombed when and did you make decisions about that too?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't -- do you mean say -- are you asking me whether targets had been prepared against this eventuality?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm asking you this: Were there cases in which you chose targets beforehand, planning air-strikes on them?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my headquarters this was not being done. I believe, but you would need to get a NATO officer to confirm or deny this, that they had prepared a number of target lists. This doesn't mean that you would attack them; it was so that you had the information available, particularly to do with air defences.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have a look at 1D635. Once we have, I'll have a question for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: We are about to see 1D635. It is a document of the State Security Service Department of Gorazde of the 2nd of July, 1995. They are reporting of the contact they had on the 1st of July, 1995, in the evening with the UNPROFOR commander. In the second paragraph they say: "On that occasion Colonel John conveyed to us that Karadzic's terrorists, in order to relieve the burden of their forces around Sarajevo, will carry out an attack in the area of Sapna and Kalesija in the course of the next few days (he didn't know what the precise date would be). The area in question is nearby Tuzla." In the last paragraph, it is stated: "We mention that -- we also mention that Colonel John Riley in a similar situation in mid-May 1995 told us that on a certain day Tuzla was to be shelled, which proved correct. We have acquainted you with that subsequently." My question is this: Did you through these British sources pass on information to the Muslims about certain things which would -- which might be taking place that you allegedly had information on?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you see here that in the last paragraph it reads: "He told us or he conveyed an information -- information to us that Tuzla would be shelled on a particular day. He was proven to be correct." And we also had this presumption that Sapna and Kalesija would come under attack and that certain measures were being planned because of that. Later on we'll see that Sapna and Kalesija were not attacked but that there was an attack from the protected area of Tuzla on the entire area of the Drina Corps, and I will present information about the casualties involved.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't see that; it's in Serb or Serbo-Croat. But I'm -- I would observe that because there is a coincidence it doesn't mean to say that there's a cause.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell the Chamber how did you know that on a particular day Tuzla would be shelled, which is why you later on applied air-strikes?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. And this document, as you're reading it to me, doesn't say I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. It says that this colonel said, this British colonel, told you that and that he had learned that -- well, I'll refer you exactly because I haven't read the entire document. This British officer is reporting to the forces in Gorazde about certain activities in Tuzla. That is why I'm asking you whether you knew and whether the British intelligence knew that on a certain day Tuzla would be shelled, which would then be used to carry out air-strikes and retaliate against Republika Srpska in areas such as Zepa.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've told you, I don't know, didn't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I want to read out the first paragraph, since we do not have a translation and I apologise for it. "We wish to inform you that on the 1st of July, 1995, in the evening we were invited to sit down by the UNPROFOR commander in Gorazde, Colonel John Riley. His explanation was that he was prepared to offer some information to us again by way of a telephone conversation with General Smith." My question is this: Did he receive the information I just referred to a moment ago through that telephone conversation with you?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I keep telling you, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Were you in telephone contact with Colonel John Riley around that time on the 1st of July, 1995; can you recall that?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think I was. I think I am on -- going on leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you know that Edward Joseph testified? He stated that many targets were bombed because the Serbs were targeting Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know he'd said that, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Again, I just want a transcript cite for that, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, can you give us -- Mr. Tolimir, can you give us a reference to a transcript page or to a document?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I asked him whether he knew that Mr. Joseph, when testifying in these proceedings, stated that some air-strikes came about --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, I know that you asked that. It is recorded. This is another question. I wanted to ask you, and I repeat it, can you give us a reference in the transcript of the testimony of Mr. Joseph?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I cannot off the cuff. If the witness does not recall that, I will not put any further questions on the topic. I just wanted to know whether he remembers it and whether he knew.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, the witness was not present when Mr. Joseph testified. If you want to put a certain part of the testimony of Mr. Joseph to the witness and ask him about this specific context, you should put that part of the transcript on the screen and then ask the witness about it. Otherwise, it's a waste of time. Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And, Mr. President, I'm in no great need to see a particular page of a transcript if we can just have some specificity as to what General Tolimir is talking about. If he's talking about air-strikes which were conducted on the 25th and 26th of May, as the Trial Chamber has heard considerable evidence about, then he can put that level of detail to General Smith, rather than generally referring to the testimony of some other witness and putting a completely vague proposition to him. He's talking about events and an alleged communication in July from a Muslim MUP report that may have some connection to May, but we can't tell from the question what he's talking about. So my request for a transcript cite can be mooted if we just have some specificity in the question itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you for this addition. In my view that was not necessary because I want to see the specific part of the transcript and especially the witness should know what the other witness testified about. Mr. Tolimir, bearing that in mind, you should continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I will bear that in mind. During the break I will find it in my notes. As you may recall, I intentionally asked him whether it was carried out because of Pale and whether the Tuzla event was in May. He said it was not. He then said that the targets were targeted in such a way. In any case, for the sake of precision, we'll find it over the break and we'll show it to General Smith, because it was stated that targets were targeted because of Tuzla later on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: To clarify this statement, I would like to know what you mean if you said "I intentionally asked him whether it was carried out because of Pale." Are you referring to this current witness, Mr. Smith, or to the other witness? I don't understand this statement.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I was referring to Mr. Joseph so as to remind the Chamber that it took place in these proceedings recently. The date of the strike was disputed and there was some discussion about whether it was because of Pale or Tuzla, and then I asked him whether the Tuzla event took place in May, and he said no, that it was in August. He was trying to point out that these were two separate events. We'll find that reference. And Mr. Thayer asked for the same thing then, to provide an exact reference. I do not object to that, but I don't wish to waste any further time until I have that reference.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: My next question is this: Did the British intelligence service forward information to the warring parties such as in this case about certain activities and plans of the enemy and whether they forwarded official information from the field to either of the sides?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was a United Nations officer and as far as I'm aware, certainly United Nations officer as the -- sorry. The United Nations and UNPROFOR did not pass information to either party about the other party. And I cannot speak for the actions of the British government in these circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Does it mean that this piece of information which he specified as having learned in a conversation with you that on a certain day Tuzla would be shelled and that an air-strike would follow, did it come from the British intelligence service or was it based on the activities in the field which you observed and conveyed to the opposing side?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've told you already, I have no idea where he got had this piece of information from or even that it is correctly reported that he had this information. And I don't think you've told me that an air-strike was to follow any of these attacks when you read out bits from this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I showed you a document referring to it. I have others in which we can see that it was this particular channel of British -- the British intelligence which was used to pass on information to the Muslim side. Was it customary to provide information to one of the parties about the other party about its military activities? And I'm asking you this because you were the UNPROFOR commander and must have been familiar with it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, the witness answered this question already, that he was a United Nations officer and that he cannot speak for the actions of the British government in these circumstances. Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. That is why I asked him whether this piece of information came from the British government or whether it was gained by UNPROFOR forces by having observed activities in the field, and he can answer with a yes or no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, the witness answered already that he can't comment on this document because he has no knowledge about it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I understand you. But his name is mentioned. The source, this British colonel, says that he was told about that by General Smith. That is why I'm asking it. In any case, I will abide by your instruction and I will move on to the next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Did you know that in the first on-site investigation in Tuzla it was concluded that the shell was fired from a distance of 21 kilometres? It struck Tuzla, causing a number of civilian casualties. Based on that, a member of the VRS was prosecuted. Did you know that?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- you've lost me completely. Which of the many cases of Tuzla being shelled are we talking about?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. The shelling of Tuzla, when it was allegedly shelled, when over 80 people were killed in the centre of town. Do you recall that event and the date?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember an actual case of Tuzla being shelled. It's associated with the bombing in May. I think it's the night of the day we first bombed the ammunition depot at Pale. And it can't have been alleged if you then prosecuted somebody. It would appear to be proven. But I didn't know that that had occurred, that is to say, the prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you know that in the first official on-site investigation, the results of which were handed over to a court, Colonel Djukic was sentenced? He is serving his sentence now. The conclusion of the investigation was that the shell came from 21 kilometres away.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you know that the Defence managed to prove that the zone of 21 kilometres was the exclusion -- within the exclusion zone and that it was actually in Muslim-held territory? It could not have come from Serb-held territory.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I don't know it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you know, then, that there was a retrial a decade later and that a new expert was engaged by a Bosnia-Herzegovina court who apparently concluded that the shell had come from a distance of 28 kilometres?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, no, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you -- do you know that the very expert testified in the Radovan Karadzic case? He was a protected witness. He was asked why ten years later he reconstructed the scene in which he established that the shell had come from a 130 millimetre cannon which was to the front of the lines.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't know it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. As a soldier, do you know that 130 millimetre cannons are never put at the front and that artillery pieces are deployed in depth to a distance at least two-thirds of range so as not to be exposed to enemy artillery fire?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that such theories abound, but I personally have moved artillery right forward into the -- with the leading elements of my attack, even on some occasions ahead of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you know that in the Karadzic case it was established that the shell was thrown off the roof of a nearby building and that on the footage it could be heard someone -- someone could be heard saying that the stabilizer fins should be brought which had been left on the roof? That was in a conversation between the people recorded.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know this about the Karadzic case.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you know that the results of investigations are still pending concerning the incident in Tuzla and that it is unknown precisely how the shell was activated or the direction from which it came? However, you seem to have used that as a basis for your conclusion to carry out air-strikes.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know that the -- that there was an investigation pending on the incident in Tuzla, and I'm at a loss to understand this is connected with a decision by me about air-strikes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, a moment ago you said that you targeted Pale over Tuzla; is that correct or have I misunderstood?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't said anything of the sort.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Did you say a moment ago that you decided to target the warehouse in Pale because Tuzla had been shelled?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't say that a moment ago. The continuing attack on the ammunition depot in Pale in May, that is to say, the second attack, was because the weapons were still not back in the weapon collection points and there had been this further shelling of the safe areas and -- of which one case of this had been the attack on Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. So there is a link between the shelling of Pale and Tuzla?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't shell Pale; I bombed an ammunition depot near Pale. And Tuzla had been attacked after I had started the bombing. And I had started it because the exclusion zone regime had broken down and my demands that the weapons were put back into the safe -- into the weapon collection points were not being heeded.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. While this document is still on the screen, can you tell us how come that you on the 2nd of July, 1995 -- sorry, the 1st of July, spoke with John Riley, and how did you know that on a certain day Tuzla would be shelled? You announced that beforehand. How are we to understand that, this announcement of yours? And it is still a number of dispute so many years after the war. Some people were prosecuted and sentenced, still serving their sentences, and many more were killed.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand how you're connecting an event that is reported to have happened that I don't know anything about on the 1st of July is connected with events that we've just been talking about which are going on at the end of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. This is what it says: "We would like to note that in a similar situation in mid-May Colonel John Riley conveyed to us information to the effect that on a certain day Tuzla would be shelled, which proved to be true, and about which we provided you with timely information." How come you know everything in advance, even individually-fired shells, and then that is used as a basis for air-strikes? Thank you. That was my question.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your question to me is wholly and utterly illogical. It is based on the assumption that the document that you have on the screen is -- that I cannot read and that you have read to me and has been translated, is actually factually correct. I have no idea whether this document is correct in what it states or not. Secondly, and even if it is -- he did warn them that this would happen in Tuzla in May and it then did happen, I do not see that the -- necessarily that there is a connection. There is maybe a coincidence, but there's no evidence of any connection whatsoever. And apart from my name being mentioned in this document, I don't see that I have a hand in it at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, we must have our first break now. And we will resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tolimir, please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I would like to move to the next document. But before that I would like to tender this one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, I have a problem with this. We don't have a translation. We don't know anything about the content except those parts you have read out in the courtroom. And this witness couldn't give any knowledge, any -- provide us with any knowledge about the content in this specific document. He said he doesn't know anything. Perhaps you should reconsider your position and offer this with another witness. I'm not sure if we have heard anything about this document, about the authenticity and the content.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Since John Riley is not going to testify and this document mentions only John Riley and this witness, maybe we could now mark it for identification because this document is very important for me. It speaks about the information at the disposal of the General, and I think that this is important. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think we can see, as the Trial Chamber has already pointed out, there are in fact two sources behind this document. It is a document emanating from the, I believe, the Bosnian MUP summarizing a conversation allegedly with this Colonel Riley who allegedly is in turn summarising a conversation he alledgedly had with General Smith. Now, there's nothing to prevent General Tolimir from calling Colonel Riley or whoever this other individual is who signed had this document. There's nothing to prevent that from happening and from Colonel Riley coming into this courtroom and testifying about this document. So to say that Colonel Reilly is not going to testify in this case is not necessarily the case. I just want to point that out so General Tolimir fully understands what his rights are as an accused in this courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. The Chamber will mark this document for identification at a later stage in this trial.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter document 1D635 shall be assigned Exhibit D188 marked for identification pending further identification. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, the Chamber would like to know the reason why you stated that Colonel Riley will not testify in this courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I said it because he is currently not on the witness list. And the only two protagonists of this event are John Riley and General Smith. General Smith said that he didn't remember this conversation and that's why I stated what I stated. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: But indeed, Mr. Thayer pointed out that Colonel Riley is not listed as a witness for the Prosecution, but we don't know anything about your Defence case yet. And if you are willing to call him or other people who could testify about this document, it is purely in your hands. You may decide by yourself. Do you want to comment on that, Mr. Tolimir?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. There is no need for me to comment anything. If it's necessary, we don't have to use this document at all. However, it is very important because it speaks about the sequence of the events that led to the bombardment. It says that information was received that on a certain day Tuzla was going to be shelled, and that's exactly what happened later. And the investigation about this is still being dragged on. So if you don't want it, I don't have anything against it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, this is not the matter we are discussing at the moment. It's only the question if you are calling any witness to testify about this document. For instance, Colonel Riley. Mr. Thayer, I saw you on your feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I suppose this is as good a time as any to offer, I think, an observation that has gained some currency in the last hour or so of General Tolimir's cross-examination. And that is, especially in the context of a self-represented accused, I think it is important that he understand that unless and until either a witness adopts something that is put to him in a proposition by General Tolimir or sheds some light on the proposition, be it from a document or from a statement from General Tolimir, or somebody connected with that document comes and testifies, then simply stating the propositions that we have heard in the last hour or so that something was concluded in the Karadzic case, for example, that there are open investigations still pending, all of these statements from the accused without being adopted in any fashion by the witness have zero evidential value. And I think it's important that he not be under any misunderstanding that when he simply makes those kinds of statements that they carry no evidential weight unless and until there is some evidence that is given by a witness in connection with the document of some sort. Because we heard a torrent of these characterisations, particularly so, I think, in the last hour referring to findings in other trials, Prosecutions, sentencings, but as yet without any factual basis whatsoever. And when we feel the need to ask for a factual bases, as the Court is aware, we get on our feet. But I just want to make sure that General Tolimir is under no misunderstanding about that fact as he continues his self-defence.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir has legal assistance. I'm quite sure that he knows about his rights and his position in this trial. Nevertheless, thank you for your position, Mr. Thayer. Mr. Tolimir. Judge Nyambe has a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: The question is to Mr. Thayer or to the Prosecution specifically. Do we know whether John Riley would be available to be present to testify in the court?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I have no idea, Your Honour. I presume if he's alive and he's of sound mind and body and he's not deployed in a hot spot that he can't get out of without reasonable notice, he would be available to either the accused or to the Trial Chamber. He's not on our list because, as you can see, this -- this document has, in our view, very, very little, if any, probative value to any issue in this case. But like any other witness, I'm sure he's available. If he's active service in particular, I think the British military has proven very co-operative in making their active and retired members available for this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. If this document is not important and has no probative value whatsoever, then why does the Prosecution stand up so much against it being tendered? Maybe we should ask General Smith once again.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Did you have a conversation with Colonel Riley, John Riley, while he was the UNPROFOR commander in Gorazde? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, I think we received the argument from the Prosecution that this witness couldn't testify about this document and therefore it is marked for identification. And the question you now put again to the witness was put to the witness already and answered.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And, Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: -- if I may, in line with our stated policy from the beginning of the trial, we've no objection to the admission of this document into evidence. My words with respect to General Tolimir's cross-examination had to do with a completely different issue, and I think everybody understands that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Go ahead, please, Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Thank you, Mr. Thayer. I have my legal assistant who can also give me advice. Thank you to everybody. I tendered this document pending the translation, of course. But if the Court deems that it is not important, we don't have to have it in evidence at all. Now I want to move on to another document. It's 1D634. Can we have in e-court 1D634. Thank you. We have it now on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: It comes from the state security sector in Gorazde, which is part of the BiH MUP, not Republika Srpska. And this document is again about the contacts between the members of this service and the members of the British forces in Gorazde. And it says: "Related to your request from the previous telegram, we hereby inform you that in order to verify our earlier information we had a conversation with Colonel Roger from BritBat. In this conversation, Roger confirmed our information that had been received from officer Allen and said that they had observed the movement of forces belonging to the aggressor whose strength was two or three brigades and which took place in the general area of Trnovo. He said that we shouldn't worry about it because his estimate is about 1.500 to 1.600 aggressor soldiers." And the last sentence: "As for the situation in Srebrenica, he said that it was stable and that no attack is expected on that enclave in the foreseeable future." Thank you. My question is: Did the British officers in Gorazde convey the information about the VRS to the BiH army? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not to my knowledge they didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. More specifically, persons mentioned in this document, did they convey any information to the BiH army related to the movements of the VRS forces? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure who they're referring to. I don't recognise the names. That doesn't mean to say they're not real people; I just don't recognise the names. And I don't know of what this report is about.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did NATO have as part of its mandate to convey the information about one warring party to the other warring party? Is that something in accordance with the NATO mandate? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't part of NATO, but I don't think it was anything to do with the NATO policy at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I apologise, I made a mistake. I was talking about the UNPROFOR mandate. Conveying the information about one warring party to the other warring party, was that part of the UNPROFOR mandate? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that wasn't what the mandate was about at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to tender this document. And, of course, it should be only marked for identification pending the translation. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, we are in the same position as with the last document. The witness couldn't say anything about this document, about the content and the authenticity. We only can mark it for identification, not pending translation, but just for identification at a later stage if you are going to use it again.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. You are, of course, aware of the fact that these documents originate from the territory of the BiH army. I cannot call any witnesses from that territory to testify on my behalf. Even the Prosecution has problems when they call witnesses from there. But to expect that they will come to testify on my behalf I don't think is going to happen. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, this is not correct. You may call every witness you need for your Defence. You may of course call witnesses who are citizens of the Republic of Serbia or of the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina or from the Republika Srpska, wherever you need to call them, you may propose them to the Chamber. It is your right. There should be no doubt about that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I would like to move on to the next document and that's the document that the witness has read.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This document on the screen will be marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter document 1D634 shall be assigned Exhibit D189 marked for identification pending further identification. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Can we now have 1D686. That's a UN document related to the heavy weaponry under the UNPROFOR control and the collection points.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: The document speaks about the zone of the exclusion of heavy weaponry. I'm interested in the third paragraph which says: "It seems today that there is no legal basis for handing back heavy weapons for use inside TEZ unless they are firing at targets inside Sarajevo city. NATO air attacks can only be used against confirmed heavy weapons within the TEZ that are not withdrawn on order or endangering the security of UNPROFOR personnel." My question is -- have you read it?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Does that mean that on the basis of this not even NATO wanted to act against the targets that did not present immediate danger for the NATO personnel or facilities protected by NATO? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, could you please help me. The first sentence you read into the record I saw on the screen; where can I find the remaining parts of your quotation?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I read the third paragraph. First we see reference, then we see A, B, and C, and what I was reading --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: That was the first paragraph.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was reading the paragraph immediately below. Immediately below C. And I read the whole paragraph. That's at least the translation that I have here at hand. That's what I can also see just below C. That's the entire paragraph that I read.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Now I see that you first read from the third paragraph on this page and then from the second paragraph. Sir, do you recall the question of Mr. Tolimir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do. Yes, I have read the whole of this document. It is an internal memorandum to the headquarters in Sarajevo. It is dated in August 1994, and it does not speak for NATO; it is saying what these staff officers who are having this internal discussion within the headquarters think NATO's -- and think the position is vis-à-vis NATO. It does not say what NATO thinks as NATO.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, bearing in mind this answer, this is my question: Was the NATO resolution binding for the warring parties and was it also verified by the Security Council?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I think I've said, I don't recall what the resolutions and their -- that were decided within the North Atlantic Council and then within the Security Council, I don't remember the steps and the chronology of these occasions. But the basis on which the exclusion zones and safe areas were set up were covered by the UN resolutions.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you remember whether the protocols that were attached to the agreement about a total exclusion zone allowed for the possibility that the warring parties could reuse the weapons that had been taken away from them in case that it was needed for their self-defence? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that that was part of the arrangement.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you remember whether VRS was attacked by the BiH army at the time? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: At what time?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: When you attacked the warehouse near Pale.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: And what are we saying? That the ... I recall that there was fighting along the confrontation line around Sarajevo that -- and that the civil population were being shelled which is why -- by weapons that had been taken out or were being used from the weapon collection points, and it was for that reason that I wished them to be, A, cease-firing, and, B, put back into the weapons collection points.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now take a look at paragraph 5; it's page 6.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Sorry, we have -- please leave -- go back to the first page of the document. Judge Nyambe has a question in relation to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Thank you. I just need some assistance to understand the relationship between UNPROFOR and NATO before I ask my next question. What was the relationship between UNPROFOR and NATO specifically in the context of this document we are looking at?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What I'm about to describe to the best of my knowledge covers not only this document but the events. The United Nations - I won't discuss the membership of the Security Council, United Nations, and NATO; I assume knowledge - was responsible for UNPROFOR and directed its actions, and the commanders of that force were under the direction of the United Nations. The NATO forces directed by the North Atlantic Council, the political body, were not stationed, with one or two exceptions, in Bosnia itself. They were conducting their operation in the skies above Bosnia. So there is a -- if you like, the one is superimposed upon the other in a spatial sense, but they are separate in their political direction and command structures. The -- I said that there were one or two members of NATO in Bosnia. The ones that -- the one that I can remember with great clarity is the liaison officer, and I think there may have been two other people with him, in my headquarters that was a direct link to the NATO headquarters in Naples, which was the overall command for the, what NATO called the southern command, essentially the Mediterranean area. Neither was in command of the other. This was a relationship that required co-ordination and co-operation and it was in -- and this was the significance of the two keys because if you've got two organisations conducting operations in and over the same space, operating to different political direction, there needed to be some means of bringing this together. And the North Atlantic Council when considering this command and control problem arrived at some time in early 1994, as I recall, but it may have been in late 1993, with this idea that you had the two keys that had to be turned but particularly in the case of the safe areas and exclusion zones. Does that answer the question? Or I can develop it further if you need me to, but if you would like to take me where you want to go, I'll try and follow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Let's see whether for the time being if I understand you correctly I'll ask you my second question. And now it's in the context of the document on the screen, where it says: "NATO air attacks can only be used against confirmed heavy weapons within the TEZ that are not withdrawn on order or endangering the security of UNPROFOR personnel."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I see that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: In your position as UNPROFOR commander, although you are not the author of this document, is that a correct categorization?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that was the situation in August 1994. This was how UNPROFOR understood the arrangements. But I recall that there was considerable tension between the NATO and UN as to this interpretation of these ideas at the time. So I think this is a -- and I'm -- that is what the staff in this headquarters, and I presume that this was being conducted in order to brief the then-commander General Rose, but it is as you can see at the back a discussion document. And the author of the document is recommending further discussion as to how this is managed and dealt with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: How was it eventually developed; do you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. You can see that by the time, nearly a year later, you have -- and I think air power has been used in the latter part of that year, the understanding of how to do this between NATO and the UN has improved, and it gets used at least two more times during the latter part of 1994. You then get the cessation of hostilities agreement and then I arrive on the scene. And as far as I'm concerned, these sorts of issues don't get raised to me again. This is one of the reasons I wanted to read the whole document is that I wasn't familiar with the -- I couldn't recall anything like this sort of discussion in my headquarters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Thank you very much for your clarification, General Smith.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, please carry on your examination.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Thank you, Judge Nyambe. Could we please show paragraph 5 on page 6 in the English version and the appropriate paragraph in English. My legal assistant says that it is actually on the screen right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I'm going to read this out in Serbian: "The protocol to the WCP agreement in Sarajevo recognizes the Bosnian Serbs' legitimate need for self-defence. If their battle positions along the confrontation line and the Serb civilian population were attacked, it is assumed that UNPROFOR would be required to intervene and use all necessary measures to stop the BiH attack," that's Bosnia-Herzegovina, "or to allow the Serbs to use their heavy weapons to defend themselves." And now this further interpretation that this person is providing: "The preferred option is to allow the Serbs to remove their heavy weapons from the TEZ either in total or in part initially and to allow their use from outside the TEZ." Now, this is my question: Since you said a moment ago that fire was coming from both sides, did the Serbs then have the legitimate right to take weapons for self-defence, as the drafter of this paragraph 5 on page 6 says?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: The -- first of all, I repeat, this is a discussion document. This has no authority as such. It is an internal discussion document within a headquarters. Secondly, I have already said that there was a recognition that there was a need for the -- for both parties to have weapons in case there was a need for self-defence. There is nothing in this that states that the weapons were to be taken without clearance by UNPROFOR.
