utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Please, why did you bomb the Serbs, then, and not the Muslims in order to stop these attacks? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told you both at the time and in this court that in -- the bombing in Pale was to have the weapons put back into the weapons collection point from which they had not been released by UNPROFOR and were being used within the exclusion zone to shell the civil population in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Were the positions of the Army of Republika Srpska being attacked from Sarajevo in these so-called total exclusion zones? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was fighting along the confrontation line, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Does that mean that the Serbs then had the right to use their very own weapons for self-defence that they had placed under your control of their own volition, provided that there are no attacks launched against them? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I repeat: The weapons were removed from the weapons collection point without any clearance by me or from UNPROFOR and they were being used to shell the civil population.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Does the protocol not say that the parties can take their weapons back for self-defence? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: My recollection was that UNPROFOR could release the weapons in cases where they were needed for self-defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Well a moment ago you said that there was fighting along the confrontation line. If there is fighting, is there not a need for self-defence? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that does not necessarily follow when you have other forces available to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Answer this then: Did you bomb the Serbs although they had the right to take weapons from weapon collection points for self-defence?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll repeat myself, I fear. I bombed the ammunition depot at Pale in -- because the weapons had been removed without any clearance from UNPROFOR from the weapon collection points and were being used to shell the civil population.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. How can you claim that it was used to target civilians when military targets were actually being hit in Sarajevo? And we will see later on in documents that they were carrying out their spring offensive from the entire zone of Sarajevo and you knew that full well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is that a question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think so. "How can you claim" was the beginning of the sentence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Right. Yes, I see that. Yes, yes. I thought it was a statement thinly disguised as a question. Because I was there and saw what was going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, could you please look at document 1D660 and then I'm going to put a question to you so that we don't spend all this time on Sarajevo because we have quite a few other questions regarding Zepa and Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the Trial Chamber please admit into evidence this document 1D686 because the witness recognised it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The witness testified about it. He didn't state that he recognised it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not recognise it, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter document 1D686 shall be assigned Exhibit D190. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could 1D660 please be displayed in e-court. Here it is on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: What we see here is that it was written on the 15th of June, 1995, information on the combat situation in the area of responsibility of the Drina Corps. It is being sent to all the units of the Drina Corps, and the first paragraph says: "The spring Muslim offensive is still underway. The Army of Republika Srpska has successfully stopped enemy break-throughs throughout the territory of the republic and created" -- "The Muslim spring offensive is still underway. The Army of Republika Srpska has successfully stopped enemy break-throughs throughout the territory of the republic and created appropriate conditions for launching counter-offensives in certain operational axes." Now, this is my question -- oh, sorry, this is a bit too loud. Did you have any knowledge about the spring offensive that the Muslims were carrying out in 1995 including the date of the 15th of June when this combat report was written? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew that they were conducting an offensive, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Please look at the second paragraph from the bottom, the last sentence there.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not in English or anything, it's in -- you'll have to read it and have it translated.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm going to translate the entire paragraph then: "Along all other axes, our forces took energetic action and thus the enemy sustained major losses and was returned to their initial positions. On this occasion, as in the case of the incursion by the sabotage group in the area of Trovrha, Debelo Brdo, and Borak hill, in the zone of responsibility of the 5th Gorazde Brigade, when the commander of the Brigade personally led the operation of breaking up the sabotage tactical group, so in the combat operations yesterday, the commanders of brigades Colonel Andric and Lieutenant-Colonel Pandurevic and the chiefs of staff of the 1st Vlasenica Light Brigade Major Sargic and the 1st Bircanska Brigade Lieutenant-Colonel Vlacic personally led the combat operations in the most endangered areas (Vis, Sokolina, Memici)." My question is the following: Did you see from this document that this spring offensive had to do with attacks from the entire part of Central Bosnia against the Drina Corps? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know necessarily. I recognise most of those names as being around -- and I'm not even sure of that now. I'd have to look at a map to be sure that I could agree with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. In that case, in order for me not to read any further documents about the losses, et cetera, and not to get maps out, tell us what you remember from that period and what you remember the Muslims having attacked during that spring offensive of theirs. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: My recollection is that the spring offensive starts in March with two large attacks, one in the west and one in the north-east. These are not particularly successful, if they are successful at all. And the next large event, in my memory, is an attack out of Sarajevo, which is occurring at about this time, middle of June.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell us, then, the bombing of the depot in Pale, was that de facto co-ordinated action with the Muslims who were attacking along the entire front line, because the NATO air force destroyed the ammunition and the reserves of the Army of Republika Srpska in that part of the front line near Sarajevo? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know what you exactly destroyed in Pale during that bombing? Or, rather, if you could tell the Trial Chamber what it was that you had targeted. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I've already done this. We attacked the ammunition depot near Pale which consisted of a number of bunkers, each in a protected band. I don't recall how many bunkers there were in the whole of the depot. The first attack was on two of the bunkers, if my memory is correct, furthest from Pale. The second was on two or maybe four, again, I can't recall, the next closest ones to Pale itself. The reason the target was chosen was that it was a military target of something that I considered and the NATO command considered was of value to the Bosnian Serbs and that it would be most unlikely, being an ammunition dump, to have any civilians in its vicinity.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please say whether it is advisable to destroy all ammunition reserves to one side when the other side is attacking them from all sides along the front line and from Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't interested in your relationship with another side. My -- this was an attack upon the Bosnian Serbs because they had broken the exclusion zone and I wanted to see, as I've explained, the shelling of the civilian population to stop and the weapons put back into the weapon collection points.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. It seems that what I said has been misinterpreted. I said whether it is necessary to destroy all the fuel and weaponry and ammunition of one warring party when it is being attacked by the other warring party; is this what the Security Council authorised you to do or not? This is something I've just added to my question now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we weren't attacking the fuel or at that point the weaponry. It was what I was authorised to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please just say -- you said a moment ago that you had been authorised, was that authority from the Security Council or from NATO?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've explained it was from the Security Council.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell the Trial Chamber on the basis of which resolution the Security Council approved of that attack that you carried out against the ammunition depot near Pale? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't recall the number of the specific Security Council resolution. I think there were some 74 that covered my -- the whole of my operation. The -- and no Security Council resolution is as specific as naming targets and time of attacks.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. As concerns all the activities of NATO and UNPROFOR vis-à-vis Republika Srpska, is that something that you managed to do on your own or did you have to have a Security Council resolution regarding each and every point in respect of every one of the warring parties? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot speak for NATO. I'm talking of myself as a UN commander. And I was operating within the Security Council resolutions that had formed the force and given its and decided its purpose.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please tell us whether the attack against Pale was retaliation or humanitarian bombing, like the one that is being applied now in NATO air-strikes against Libya? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not going to make any comparisons with Libya. This is occurring some 16 years ago. It was as I have said, to achieve the cessation of the bombing -- of the shelling of the civil population in the safe area of Sarajevo and for the return of the weapons into the weapon collection point.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. We saw in item 5 that the side that is under attack had the right to withdraw their weapons from the collection points in order to defend itself. How does that tally with your decision to bomb the same side? Did you bomb the Muslim positions used to target Serb civilians and RS territory?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, as we have only the B/C/S text on the screen and this is from the command of the Drina Corps, I'm not sure that this statement is really correct which you put to the witness. Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And in any event, Mr. President, I've lost count of how many times this question has been asked and answered. It's been asked in different forms, different ways, from different directions, but is it the same question and the same answer has been provided innumerable times.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, I'm quite sure that you will receive always the same answer to your questions on this specific matter. You should be aware of the time you have at your disposal for concluding your cross-examination. Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Did you carry out humanitarian bombing of the RS in the period of time when you bombed Pale?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not understand what you mean by "humanitarian bombing."

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, you said that you wanted to protect the civilian population but from that very area where the civilians lived, attacks came against the RS. Did you, therefore, justify your decision by humanitarian bombing, much as is done nowadays when NATO is justifying its bombing of Brindisi [as interpreted] and [as interpreted] Libya, and this also includes the forces of France?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, this is not a correct way of conducting your cross-examination. You should stop comparing the events in Bosnia with nowadays events in other parts of the world. The witness answered your question several times about the reason why the bombing on the ammunition depot near Pale was carried out. Please go ahead with your questions and move to another topic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. However the link is very strong because all bombings carried out by NATO in Republika Srpska and in Serbia and in Iraq and in Libya and in Afghanistan have to do with --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I have to interrupt you, Mr. Tolimir. I gave you this guide-line yesterday and today again. That might be your position. That is a fair point. You may deal with that but not to put this area and these historical events to this witness. He is testifying here about the events in Bosnia-Herzegovina and nothing else. Please carry on and move to another topic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We will then move to Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Did the forces which carried out the bombing of RS -- of the RS support Bosnia-Herzegovina's secession from the then joint state of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you referring to NATO?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Well I think the bombing was carried out by UNPROFOR, and NATO merely used its military force.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what I want to understand. So you're asking me whether the United Nations supported the secession of Bosnia-Herzegovina from Yugoslavia; is that your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I asked you whether the forces which bombed the RS supported Bosnia's secession from the federal state of Yugoslavia to which Bosnia-Herzegovina belonged prior to the secession.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: The forces I represented and commanded in Bosnia in 1995 had no political position whatsoever. We were there, amongst other reasons, to conduct the safe area policy, the exclusion zones, and so forth in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Then perhaps you can tell us why only the Serbs were bombed in Bosnia-Herzegovina and in all of Yugoslavia which existed before this secession. Why were only the Serbs bombed and not the rest?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because the Bosnian Serbs gave cause by attacking the civil population in the safe areas and by removing their weapons from the weapon collection point.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Yesterday you said that you were on official business in NATO when the people of Serbia were bombed. Can you tell us why Serbia was bombed for 78 days? Why? I certainly wouldn't like others to enjoy the same fate.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was -- you are now referring to the Kosovo operation; is that what I am to understand?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, you understood it well. You bombed all of Yugoslavia, Zemun, the bridges over the Danube, which had nothing do with Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I have to remind you, Mr. Tolimir, that the witness is here to testify as a representative of the United Nations at the time in Bosnia-Herzegovina in 1995. Not to testify in his later position as a NATO official in 1999. This is a waste of time to deal with the Kosovo conflict here in this trial. Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. It is important to point out the continuity of bombing Serbs as a nation. It is very important. If only the Serbs are being bombed in Bosnia and then in Serbia, then there must have been a reason for doing so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Again, Mr. President, our position is we don't have any objection to this line of questioning, given General Smith's experience, if the answer -- or the question isn't asked 18 times. If we have -- we have no objection to it being answered once. And if it's answered, then it's left alone, and then it's not repeated over and over and over again with the same answer being elicited.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. In that case, I won't ask any further questions. I wanted to ask this of the witness because he held a position in the North Atlantic Treaty Organisation during the bombing of Yugoslavia and Serbia. It wasn't by accident that I asked him that, but because he held that position. I seek to tender this document pending translation. Thank you. It refers to the Muslim spring offensive which was confirmed by the witness. And if we admit that, I won't have a need to go into the number of casualties and the areas covered by the offensive specifically.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Can we please see the next page of this document. What is the basis, Mr. Tolimir, to tender this document which we can't read, that is one point, during the examination of the Witness Rupert Smith? He explained his and he told us his knowledge about the spring offensive and what he recalled. We don't see any relation to this document to this witness. I have a problem with that. You may call other witnesses to testify about that. At least we should have first a translation so that we can judge on that, otherwise we should only mark it for identification and we will wait for a later time to check it. Are you in agreement with that?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I wish to continue. I would like to ask e-court --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, 65 ter document 1D660 shall be assigned Exhibit D191 marked for identification pending translation and further identification. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we please look at 1D655. It is General's statements provided on the 12th of January, 2005. He provided that information to the Dutch Institute for War Documentation, or the NIOD. We're interested in page 1, paragraph 2, in which the General says the following. Paragraph 2, we have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: The General says: "It is obvious that some information came by way of national channels, but he specified that there was no national prioritization of tasks and that is why there was no optimal national input. The only source Smith had at his disposal were the JCOs. His personnel or staff was dysfunctional because the members of the staff received orders from their --"

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we turn to the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: -- "from their capital cities." My question is this: Could you explain to the Chamber how you verified or checked such data received through national channels to see whether they are credible and whether they reflected the interest of the providing nations participating in the UN operation?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can I see the whole of the paragraph in the English, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Have a look at the rest of paragraph 2 of your statement.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: This report is -- is someone summarising a long conversation that I had with the team that visited. It's their -- if you like, their product from these -- this conversation, and I haven't -- I've seen it before, but I never saw it before it was printed and produced. You are -- the question was, again? Yes. I draw a distinction here, and this is, I think, comes out in that paragraph. I'd like to draw a distinction between information and intelligence. And I've used and am in the habit of using the two words differently. Intelligence being a subset, if you like, of information. And you did get information from capitals; you were visited by people from capitals; your troop-contributing nations or the representatives of those troop-contributing nations would visit you, well, the military, and so forth; and you had information in that -- from those sources. And of course, all of this was put in the balance and checked with what was going on around us, just as we were briefing back to the -- these people when they were visiting us but also to the -- our own superior headquarters in Zagreb. The -- and the more a specific a nation was about its interest, and I've referred to the British in Gorazde, the more you tended to hear about that interest and that particular place because they had a detachment or a -- or a unit in that vicinity.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did members of the staff at UNPROFOR command receive or could they receive orders from their capitals? because it says here that they did. It was the last sentence of my quote in the first paragraph or the first part of the paragraph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Can we go back to the previous page, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't think it did say that. I specifically state that there was no national tasking.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Please look at paragraph 1. It says here that "Smith received intelligence from the US and NATO." Here they have in mind specific intelligence. Could you please explain the entire sentence, bearing that in mind?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Unfortunately we have two paragraphs number 1. Are you referring to the first number 1 or the second number 1?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I think I said that we should look at paragraph 1 where we see the mention of NATO and the US. I meant the first first paragraph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It is that sentence which is marked by, yes, the cursor. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Again, I'm not the author of this or nor did I sign it or see it when it was written, but it seems to me that the author is running together answers to a number of questions that that were specifically to -- or the answers were specific to certain times in my time in Bosnia rather than a more general observation. And to explain: A, you can see the point I've made already that I think there's a difference between intelligence and information. That the -- and as I've said, NATO was the organisation doing the targeting, that is to say, the specific business of working out how to attack a target, what it looked like so that the pilots and so forth could be briefed. And that then I think he's run something else together in that, as the Court knows, I was involved in the British Ministry of Defence, and the job I had before I went to Bosnia I was the -- on the staff in the Ministry of Defence and one of my responsibilities was the British contribution to this operation in the Balkans, to the UN operation in the Balkans. And so I'm now saying, I think, that -- and what he's run together into one paragraph, is that I had some understanding of what was happening from British sources when I was sitting at my desk in London. This was not available to me by the time I get into Bosnia in 1995 in January. And I then build up this hypothesis which you've heard about.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. In that case, please look at paragraph 3.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to ask e-court to show us paragraph 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: It reads: "At our repeated insistence, supported by examples to the effect that there was available intelligence at Codeword Cobalt level (by the way, he made a note of this), Smith asserted it decidedly: 'There were no forewarnings regarding an imminent attack on Srebrenica.'" My question is this: Did you receive warnings and available intelligence as you said here as part of Codeword Cobalt? And perhaps you can explain to the Chamber what it stands for.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: It doesn't say I received forewarnings in this paragraph. It says the opposite. And to this day I don't know what Codeword Cobalt is or means.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. In that case, can you tell us this: When we look at paragraph 2 where you mentioned the JCO, please explain to the Bench what it stands for, what its role was as part of UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: The JCOs were part of UNPROFOR. They were deployed -- they were a British unit deployed from -- in -- sorry, not from, in 1994, I think. And they -- their name stands for -- the -- there was a Joint Commission, and I can't remember which of the cease-fires it was that this first -- this phrase joint title, this Joint Commission, becomes used, but these people were initially employed to act as the observers and to inform a Joint Commission over the efficacy and the handling of the cease-fire that had been agreed. As I say, this occurred in 1994 in the time of my predecessor General Rose. They -- their role developed and they were -- because they travelled and were able to move across the confrontation lines, they were a useful source of information, particularly as they were also talking on a fairly regular basis to the Bosnian Serbs again in particular around Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Since it was a British unit, was it answerable to the British armed forces or only to the British UNPROFOR commander?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were answerable to the UNPROFOR commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Was Mr. Wood a member of the unit?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: It depends what time we're asking. He was certainly a member of the JCOs, and I think you're referring to a Major Wood at the time, in -- during the summer of 1995. I can't remember when his tour ended.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us whether he received his salary from the British forces, since it was a British unit, or for from the UN? And also, who would pay any indemnity or benefits should anything have happened to him?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps it would help if I answered this, this command and control question, fairly fully. Every -- the position of the UN when it wants to form -- the Security Council had decided to form the force is that it appeals to the member nations of the UN to provide forces. These forces rest that they provide, they then become called the troop-contributing nations or a nation. Of course, the forces that they provide owe their standing, their origins, and their legal position as a soldier to that state and its laws. And that state is responsible for them as a soldier, as a profession. They would pay him or her and so forth. The UN, in cases where a nation finds it extremely difficult to provide the forces because of the state of their economy, will provide funds that help pay the soldier for this foreign service and the alliances and so forth. But in a military sense, this is understood by the use of a certain nomenclature and principles. And we talk, in the military, and this would apply to most nations, they will -- the words might change slightly, but generally the command rests with the legal-founding authority. And therefore the command in a full sense of the word for his discipline, welfare, payment, and ultimate purpose rests with the state that he comes from. And you then hand either command or control to the other authority that you've handed them to, and there's whole gradations of this as to how much you hand over in the specific purposes. And from my memory, the troop-contributing nations were placing their forces under the UN command under the heading of operational control, by which it means that you can assign missions to them, tell them what to do and they are to do it, but they -- but the authorities for paying them, disciplining them, and so forth remains with the parent state.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you for that. We must have our first break now -- second break now. And we will resume five minutes past 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Smith, we discussed the JCOs; and in relation to this, my question is: Were you the only one who issued orders to Mr. Wood in his position of the commander of the unit in order for him to be able to perform his duties and carry out his tasks? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. To carry out his duties and tasks in relation to UNPROFOR, I was the one who gave him the orders, yes. Or they came from me, the orders that he received.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Your superior in Zagreb, was he able to issue orders to him? Or on the other hand, was maybe one of your subordinates able to issue orders to him, such as Gobillard? Or did all orders have to come from you?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: My superior would have, if he wanted something done, he would have requested that of me and I would have decided who and how it was done. General Gobillard when he was acting as my deputy in my absence could give orders to the JCOs because he was acting as commander of UNPROFOR. And if I had placed a JCO detachment into someone else's command, then in the way I have described of how one can pass your formation, your organisations, down the hierarchy of command, then in those particular -- for those particular circumstances that commander could have given orders to a JCO detachment.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Since you call them Joint Commission Observers, could you tell us, were they the only ones within the UNPROFOR structure who guided the planes in order for them to reach their targets? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. There were forward air control parties for this purpose.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Were they also used to guide the planes? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: JCOs could and did act as forward air controllers.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. And one more question on the same subject. When they were in a situation to guide the planes, were the land observers, including the JCOs, in a formation with the planes, military speaking, or could we say that they were the eyes and ears of the planes on the ground?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not clear who these land observers you are including with the JCOs; who are they?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. If people who were the members of JCOs were in a situation where they could guide the plane, engage in an action against, say, a Serbian tank in Gorazde or Srebrenica, did they have then a direct relation to targeting devices who were actually performing the targeting? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: If they were acting as a forward air controller, yes, they were communicating with the aircraft or, rather, with the pilot in the aircraft.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In order to act expeditiously, I would like to tender this document. It's 1655. His statement given to the NIOD. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This is the wrong number. It is 1D655. This document will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter document 1D655 shall be assigned Exhibit D192. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we now have in e-court D147. 174, I apologise. D174. It's a memo sent by Mr. Akashi to Mr. Annan, and among the recipients we find the name of General Smith. I would like to look at paragraph 2. More precisely, 2(b).

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: The subject is UNPF policy and information for the Security Council. Thank you. Mr. Smith, this document is dated the 11th of July. You received it. And it defines the UNPROFOR policy; we can find that in the subject line. Were all the structures within UNPROFOR bound to act in accordance with the policy defined here? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can we go to the beginning of the document. I'd like to know what is -- it is. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And could it be, please, enlarged a bit.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay, you can turn.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Can you give us your answer based on the first page. And the question was: Were all the UNPROFOR structures bound to act in accordance with this policy? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm still trying to understand what the policy is, so I can't answer your question. And what it appears, from the preambular paragraph, is that this is informing Annan of what -- as to his intentions. I don't know what these intentions fully are yet until you -- I'm allowed to read the second page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Smith, if you permit me, I'm going to ask questions based on what I can read. Because if you're going to read the whole document, we are going to lose lots of time. It's a large document, similar to many other documents from UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, but you're asking me to talk about a policy. I can't answer your question till I know what the policy is and therefore can then answer the question as to whether or not everyone was bound to act by it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'd simply ask that General Smith be given the courtesy that every other witness before this Trial Chamber has. He's asked to have an opportunity to read a document which the accused wishes to put to him. And if he needs extra time to do that, then we can perhaps give General Smith some more homework that he can do at a break. And when he's had an opportunity to read it, he can then answer the question. But to blame General Smith and then claim he doesn't have a lot of time, I think, is not helpful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I have nothing against General Smith reading all the documents tendered by me. But I simply thought because, for instance, here my question is based solely on the subject where it says the UNPROFOR policy and that's all that my question pertains to, nothing else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The witness answered: "But you're asking me to talk about a policy. I can't answer your question unless I know what the policy is and therefore can then answer the question," and so on. You received this answer. It's not helpful just to repeat it but you should rephrase it or give the witness the opportunity to read the whole document whenever this is possible. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Then I'm going to move to my following question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Was UNHCR bound to observe the UN policy? Did this policy also pertain to UNHCR? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: UNHCR are mentioned. And, of course, if the UN has a policy, then its subordinate organisations are trying to follow it. But as I pointed out at the beginning, this document looked like, from the preambular paragraph, a -- more a discussion as to what Mr. Akashi intended to do than an expression of UN policy. And we can turn again. Thank you. On this one very quick read, I don't think this is in itself a policy document. It is a discussion document about policy, and Mr. Akashi is reporting to his superior in New York the situation on the ground as at 11th of June. He is describing the problems that he faces, and he's proposing or suggesting that he might do certain things. And if this is to be done, he would like the Security Council to take certain actions which he lists. And he then -- and he finishes by asking for the -- all business of the safe areas to be reconsidered or in the United Nations and their commitment to this idea. And he has sent this to his subordinates, of which I am one, so that we understand the nature of the debate as to our future that is going on around us. To that extent, I for one when I read this, which I imagine I did although I don't recall doing so, would have taken my own decisions in the knowledge that this debate was going on and what Mr. Akashi was proposing to Mr. Annan.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: May I draw your attention to item 6 on the screen, the last paragraph.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Does it show which kind of document this is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it does. It is a discussion document in the sense of informing his superior. He's going to keep him closely informed both of developments on the ground as well as how our thinking develops in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Can you now take a look at item (b) on page 2. I'm going to read the relevant part. You can see it now, and it says: "UNHCR reports that 80 to 90 per cent of the population of Srebrenica (total population is 40.000) are displaced persons who fled fighting earlier in the war. Thus they do not have long-standing ties to homes and property in the enclave and will probably be interested in leaving for Tuzla. A UNHCR local staff member in Srebrenica reported today that virtually everyone in the enclave wishes to leave. The UNHCR SE will discuss this issue as well as immediate humanitarian requirements in a meeting tomorrow in Tuzla with the Bosnia Minister for Refugees Mr. Cero. Following consultations with the Bosnian government and in order to avoid the continuing humanitarian catastrophe, agreement will be solicited from the Bosnian Serbs to allow all residents of Srebrenica, including all men, to leave for Tuzla if they so wish. The Dutch will be instructed to remain in the Srebrenica enclave at least until arrangements have been negotiated and finalised with Bosnian Serb authorities for the departure from the enclave of those people. Ideally, UNPROFOR will maintain an armed and substantial presence in the enclave at least until the departure from the enclave of all those wishing to leave has been completed. This preference will need to be balanced ..." And so on and so forth. My question is: Did UNPROFOR command have this information by UNHCR which, as we can see, was sent by Akashi to you? So did you receive information contained within this paragraph, more specifically, that all the inhabitants wished to leave Srebrenica? Did you know about that? I mean, you people who were deciding about the events that were to follow.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I've said, I'm sure we received this document, and while I don't recall the precise figures or anything like that, I'm -- I was quite clear that the population wished to leave Srebrenica after the enclave had collapsed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know whether VRS or, more specifically, General Mladic was requested to permit the evacuation of all the inhabitants of Srebrenica? Did anybody from UNPROFOR request that? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall that. And it may have happened before I got back from leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, in that case, can we take a look at P991. It's the Srebrenica video that I want to see, from 46:29 -- from 46:23 to 48:29. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, we have still on the screen the document D174. That is not an exhibit yet. It was tendered through the Witness Edward Joseph. It was at that time marked for identification and you were given the opportunity to tender it through the current witness, Mr. Smith. Are you tendering it now?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course. Thank you, Mr. President. But we should also keep it close at hand because we are going to use it later on again. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received as an exhibit, as D174. Mr. Tolimir, you may continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now have the Srebrenica video, from 46:23 to 48:29. That's P991. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: You were not present there, but you now had the opportunity to see it. My question is: Did Colonel Karremans in accordance with the orders that he mentioned, orders that came from the UNPROFOR command for Bosnia and from the UNPROFOR command for Sarajevo, was he tasked to take care of the refugees and also to get in contact with the Serbian side in relation to their situation? Did he do that in accordance with your instructions? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: What date was this record -- this video made?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. The video was made in the evening hours of the 11th. That's when Mr. Karremans invited General Mladic. Thank you. And you saw that at the beginning General Mladic said, Here I am, what do you want? You requested me to come here.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I saw that bit. I wanted to know what the date was. He is clearly saying that he received those orders. I have said to you I wasn't present in my headquarters on that day and I don't know in any great detail what orders were issued by the Bosnian -- I'm sorry, the headquarters in Sarajevo, the UN headquarters in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Please, from the moment when General Mladic accepted what Karremans had asked him for, why did the UN change its rhetoric? Why did they say that it was Mladic who carried out forcible movements of the population and when all of this is written in all the documents that Mr. Annan and you and everybody else in UNPROFOR commands knew about, and in the UN? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: All of what is written? That Mladic forcibly removed the population? Or that Karremans said this to camera on the 11th of July?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: This is what I'm asking you. Is Karremans telling General Mladic on behalf of the civilians that they had requested to be evacuated; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: My memory of the video is that he, Karremans, is asking to negotiate, or asked, for the conditions for the -- to get the people out.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, because it is that way, why was the rhetoric changed later by UNPROFOR? And why is it being said all the time that Mladic arbitrarily carried out this evacuation from Srebrenica, of the Muslims from Srebrenica, whereas he was the one who had asked him to do that? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you show me where everybody is saying that this didn't happen and Mladic forcibly evacuated everybody? What I think everybody is saying, to the contrary, is that Mladic carried out this attack that led to this situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did the attack from this demilitarised zone against Mladic's population and army cause that attack and he as commander was supposed to protect that population and his own troops?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was one of the reasons for carrying out the attack. It was a -- it could be understood as the proximate cause of the attack.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. That's why I'm asking you, why was the rhetoric changed? If in the beginning UNPROFOR is asking for evacuation, why is it later on being replaced by the term "deportation" or something like that when it was actually what UNPROFOR had been asking for? I'm asking you, why this change in the rhetoric?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't answer the reason for the -- what you call the rhetoric. I would need to be given an example of what you're talking about. But what I can say is that UNPROFOR is asking for an evacuation because of the consequences of the attack by Mladic's forces and the mass refugees it had created specifically around the Dutch position at Potocari.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Please tell us whether you heard in this part of the video when Mr. Karremans says that the Dutch would be given instructions to stay in the enclave until the departure of these people from the enclave is organised? Thank you. Did you hear that part? Did you hear him speaking about that?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that bit in the video, but that, indeed, as you can see from the other document you've shown me, was what Mr. Akashi had wanted.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. In that case, I don't want us to go through all these documents yet again, but could you just please tell us whether an instruction had been issued to the Dutch Battalion to stay in the enclave until they are given other instructions? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think it was couched in those terms. The instructions were to look after the refugees and see to their -- to their evacuation with Mladic, and then your, the Dutch, evacuation would be considered.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. In that case, tell us, please, did anyone in UNPROFOR ever look at the following possibility: That members of UNPROFOR in Srebrenica, in this case the Dutch, stay on in Srebrenica together with the civilian population after the army, as we had seen, left Srebrenica, and was that option ever offered to the population, to the Army of Republika Srpska, and UNPROFOR? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, the option wasn't. It was a wholly impractical option. We couldn't have fed all those refugees or housed them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Wouldn't have been -- wouldn't it have been reasonable for these people to have stayed at their homes and in the territory where they had lived and then to have the Army of Republika Srpska and UNPROFOR protect them? because, after all, the Army of Republika Srpska had asked for the demilitarisation of Srebrenica. Was that ever offered? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: The people in -- those refugees did not want to be protected by the Bosnian Serb army. They did not trust the Bosnian Serb army. They were very frightened of the Bosnian Serb army, which is why they were all clustered around the Dutch base in Potocari.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Perhaps I misspoke or perhaps I was misinterpreted. Was this variant ever looked at: That UNPROFOR protect the population in the territory where they lived, in their villages and houses, whereas the Army of Republika Srpska would not enter the zone because they had actually asked for its demilitarisation? Thank you. Would that have been one of the reasonable solutions, as I think it would have been? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I think that would have been wholly impractical in the circumstances of 11th of July and thereafter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, we must come to an end for the day. Could you give us your estimation of the remaining time you need for concluding your cross-examination? I think you used 9 hours and 40 minutes, approximately the time during cross.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I think that I'm going to finish within the time that we had asked for. I don't think I'm going to ask for any extension of time, which is not to say that that will never be the case with other witnesses. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir, yesterday I asked you if you would perhaps be available next week for continuation of your examination.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As promised, I've made some -- I've rearranged things. I can be here for all of Monday afternoon's session. But I'm not available, at least not with any ease, for the rest of the week. I've pushed the events of -- planned events of Monday into Tuesday and then I'm supposed to be in another country altogether on -- at the end of this week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The Chamber appreciates your co-operation. Thank you for that. I think I can promise you that your testimony will be concluded the next day of the hearing, that means on Monday.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: If there's nothing else -- no. Mr. -- I see Mr. Gajic on his feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I would just have a small request for the Trial Chamber. I think that yesterday or the day before yesterday you did have some praise for Courtroom I in view of these proceedings. The Defence would kindly ask that this courtroom be used only if it is absolutely necessary. I think we have strong reasons for that. As for this place where Mr. Tolimir is sitting and also the place where he spends his time during the break, he is handcuffed and a different procedure is applied. I've had the opportunity of seeing that yesterday. Also, the climate, as it were, is a bit unpleasant in this seat where Mr. Tolimir is sitting. So if the Trial Chamber accepts our suggestion that we go on in Courtroom III or in Courtroom II, well, of course if necessary we can conduct hearings in Courtroom I, we will not be opposed to that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much for this submission. We will take that into account. But at the moment there is no need for any decision in this respect because we are scheduled to sit in Courtroom III in the next week and the following weeks, as I am aware of. Thank you very much to everybody. And we have to adjourn now and resume on Monday, 2.15, in Courtroom III.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
